chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 291 to 300, Kapilar's peacock decade (மஞ்ஞைப் பத்து) of kurinji: each poem sets the hill's peacock beside the hill girl, through the secret love (the man's longing, the friend's fear of his night visits, the girl's heart gone with him) to the wedding, and by the end the peacock is likened to the girl rather than she to it.

291.reading: The man points out the hill slope of piled boulders where peacocks dance and the owl calls back and forth, and says that is the fine town where his beloved lives, the girl with shoulders like bamboo and a waist where a skirt of chosen leaves sways.
291.nuance: The poem names nothing but a place, yet the place is all lover's sight: the dancing peacocks and the calling owl are the sounds he hears around her town, and the leaf skirt on her waist is the one ornament of the hill girl.

thinai_evidence.note: a slope of piled boulders where peacocks dance

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, full and smooth as bamboo

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of 'my beloved' (காதலி) and points to her town (அதுவே); the companion as addressee is a guess

292.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hill embraced by cool rain clouds, where peacocks dance and big bees hum, that the girl is dearer to them than he is, for by holding in desire the strictly guarded wedding in the good house he has given them back their own well-being, and she is now theirs for good.
292.nuance: The friend's praise of the bride is also a claim on her: the girl the man has married is more precious to her own circle than the man, and their own welfare (எம்நலம்) rose with the wedding, so the secret love's anxiety is over for the friend as much as for the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: peacocks and bees of the rain-clouded hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; someone who says 'us' (எமக்கே, எம்நலம்) of the bride and addresses the groom after the wedding, most likely the friend

293.reading: The man asks the girl who covered his eyes with her lovely hand, like a fragrant cluster of kanthal that scents the hillside, the maiden of bamboo shoulders with the grace of a peacock who has become his sweet companion of the bed, whether anyone but her dwells in his heart.
293.nuance: The game of covering his eyes from behind asks 'guess who'; his answer turns the game into a vow, since there is no one else it could be. The flower of the hand is the kanthal, the hill's own flower, so she is praised with things of her land.

thinai_evidence.note: the kanthal that scents the hillside

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man answers the woman who covered his eyes; பாயல் இன்துணை, companion of the bed, suggests wedded life

294.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the peacock perched on the fire-bright vengai looks like a jewelled maiden that he has done a sweet thing, and blesses his father, for holding the wedding in the good house and setting flowers in the girl's thick braided hair.
294.nuance: The simile already shows the wedding before the friend names it: a peacock dressed in the vengai's red-gold blossoms is a bride dressed in jewels, and the last line has the man himself dress her hair with flowers. The blessing on his father (நுந்தை வாழியர்) praises the man through his lineage, as one praises a good family's son. That the peacock and the bride make a hidden comparison is ruled out by the marker -இன், which states it.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock on the flowering vengai

comparisons.tenor: the peacock perched on the vengai

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; someone who speaks of the bride as இவள் and thanks the groom for the wedding, most likely the friend

295.reading: The girl asks whether her heart, which went off with the man of the hill country, where the peacock, driven by the field-clearers' firebrands, rushes out like girls at ball play and harries the sparrows on the millet stubble, will come back, or will settle there because it wants to live with him.
295.nuance: The question is put to no one: she cannot recall the heart and does not know its mind. The picture of the startled peacock scattering the sparrows like girls chasing a ball is lively play beside her stillness; reading it as a hidden image of her own unsettled heart would need more than one match, so it is left as scene. Line 3 (புனவர் கொள்ளியின் புகல்வரும்) may mean the peacock flees the firebrands or comes eagerly toward them.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country's peacock, millet stubble and field-clearers

comparisons.tenor: the peacock's rush among the sparrows

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the girl speaks of 'my heart' that went with the hill man; the friend as hearer is a guess, the poem may be spoken to no one

296.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the slope's peacock steals the heavy-eared millet the hill girl guards that he comes even in the dark of midnight, and that if a fierce beast should strike him she would not know what to do.
296.nuance: The refusal is made as fear for him, not as blame. The opening scene does double work: the guarded millet stolen by the peacock is the guarded girl he takes in secret, and the millet field is also where the girls are by day, a hint of where he might meet her instead of at midnight.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl guarding millet and the night visit

comparisons.tenor: the man who takes the guarded girl in secret

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the speaker tells the man he comes at midnight and fears for him, the friend's refusal of the night tryst

ullurai.tenor: the guarded girl and the man who comes for her by night

pairs.situation: the girl is kept under guard by her household
the man takes her love in secret, slipping past that guard

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the millet field and peacock of the kurinji hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

297.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the peacock on the great bough of the spreading vengai looks like women plucking flowers that even if he goes away, the love of the girl who has joined with him will not go away.
297.nuance: The play on பிரி (part) carries the poem: his parting is one thing and her bond's parting another, and the second will not follow the first. It is an assurance, but also a reminder that the bond holds her whether or not he returns.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock on the flowering vengai of the hill; the parting is the short one of secret love, not a journey

comparisons.tenor: the peacock among the vengai blossoms

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the speaker tells the man about 'the maiden joined with you', so not the girl herself; the friend, as he is about to leave

298.reading: The man says that though the slow-gaited hill girl of the good town on the slope, where peacocks dance without knowing whether rain will come, shows him no grace, he has never once forgotten her, thinking of her always.
298.nuance: உள்ளுபு மறந்தறியேம், 'thinking of her, we have never known forgetting', is the same turn the Kural gives the man in 1125. The peacock that dances before any sign of rain is the man who keeps loving before any sign of her favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the dancing peacock of the hill slope and the hill girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of a girl who does not favour him (அருளாள்); speaking to her friend to win her help is a guess

iraicchi.act: the peacock dances in hope though it does not know that the rain will come
iraicchi.sense: the man keeps the girl in his thoughts and loves on, though no sign of her grace has come

299.reading: The man says that the split-mouthed blue lilies blooming in the green spring on the hill-man's slope can hardly open like the eyes of the slow-gaited hill girl with her fine thin locks, and that even the peacock can hardly have her soft grace.
299.nuance: The comparison is turned round: the lily and the peacock, the hill's usual likenesses for eyes and grace, are measured against her and fall short. Both come from her own hill (குன்ற நாடன் குன்றத்து), so it is her land's best that she outdoes.

thinai_evidence.note: the lily of the hill spring and the peacock

comparisons.tenor: the blue lilies, which cannot open as her eyes do
the peacock, which cannot have her grace

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man praises the girl as இவள், one present or near; he names the hill as குன்ற நாடன் குன்றத்து in the third person, read here as her father the hill chief; the friend as addressee is a guess, and the friend as speaker is possible

300.reading: The friend tells the girl of sweet words that the lord of the great-rocked hill, where the peacock spreads its lovely plumes like a hill girl's hair, has come, and her kin have agreed to give her to him: may her good fortune flourish.
300.nuance: The decade closes with the marriage settled. Here the peacock is likened to the girl, not she to it: by the end of the decade she is the standard the hill's birds are measured by.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock of the great-rocked hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the speaker brings the girl (அம்தீம் கிளவி) news that the man has come and her kin agreed to the marriage, the friend's announcement

links.note: Both give the man the same words for constancy: Kural 1125 உள்ளுவன் ... மறப்பறியேன், answering the friend who asks whether he remembers; Ainkurunuru 298 உள்ளுபு மறந்தறியேமே, said of a girl who shows him no grace.
links.teaches: The Kural's joke that he cannot remember what he never forgets answers a doubt about absence, while the Ainkurunuru sets the same claim against her coldness, so together they show the man's never-forgetting was the stock answer to both doubts the friend tests him with: will he stay away, and will he give up if she is unkind.

links.note: Both have the man say the blue water-lily (குவளை) cannot match the girl's eyes: Ainkurunuru 299 says the lily of her own hill spring can hardly open as her eyes do, and Kural 1114 that the lily, if it could see, would bow its head ashamed.
links.teaches: The Ainkurunuru states the defeat of the lily as a plain fact of the girl's own hill, and the Kural gives the lily sight and a modest bowed head, so the pair shows the Kural's conceit growing out of the akam habit of measuring the hill girl against her land's flowers, with the lily now made to act out her own modesty.

links.note: Both have the woman speak of her heart that has gone after the man: in Ainkurunuru 295 she wonders whether the heart that went with the hill man will come back or settle there; in Kural 1248 she calls her heart foolish for following the one who left, pining that he will not show grace.
links.teaches: The Kural judges the following heart a fool because the man has gone and withholds his grace, while the Ainkurunuru girl, with no doubt of him, only wonders whether her heart will return, so the pair shows that the same act of the heart going after the man is not folly in itself and is judged by how the man answers it.

links.note: Both have the friend bid the hill lord not come at midnight for fear of beasts: Ainkurunuru 296 in four lines, fearing a fierce beast; Akananuru 92 with a tiger striking an elephant, and then the offer that tomorrow she and the girl will be guarding the millet, where he may meet her by day (பகற்குறி, the colophon says, to press marriage).
links.teaches: Akananuru 92 spells out the day tryst at the millet field, which shows that the opening of Ainkurunuru 296, the millet the hill girl guards, is not idle scenery but the same unspoken offer, so the short poem's refusal of the night already points to where and when he may come.

links.note: Both turn on the girl's hand laid on the man's eyes: in Natrinai 28 the girl recalls how in the secret love he took her hand and pressed it to his eyes, then left her like a thief; in Ainkurunuru 293 the wife covers his eyes from behind in play and he says no one else lives in his heart.
links.teaches: In Natrinai 28 the hand on his eyes was his gesture of a promise that his leaving made false, while in Ainkurunuru 293 it is her game in the married bed that draws from him the vow of no other, so the pair shows the same touch losing its doubt once the promise of secret love has been kept in marriage.

source_issues: Every colophon of the decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
295 line 3 புனவர் கொள்ளியின் புகல்வரும் மஞ்ஞை: புகல் may be the peacock's fear of the field-clearers' firebrands or its eagerness; the poem's sense does not turn on it.
298 line 1 மழைவரவு அறியா may be 'not knowing the rain will come' or 'not knowing (whether) rain comes'; the iraicchi reading holds on either.
Repaired lines flagged by show (293 lines 1 and 3, 294 line 5, 295 line 1, 298 line 4, 299 line 1) were read as repaired; no further doubt.
